question.text: According to the common age-based rule of thumb for asset allocation, what should be the approximate equity allocation for a 35-year-old investor?

explanation.text: The Logic: The widely cited age-based rule of thumb for asset allocation states: Equity allocation (%) = 100 - Age. Applying this to a 35-year-old investor: 100 - 35 = 65%, so approximately 65% in equity and the remaining 35% in debt and other asset classes. The intuition is that younger investors have a longer horizon to absorb equity volatility, so they can take more equity risk. The Trap: Using age directly as the equity allocation (35% equity for a 35-year-old) inverts the rule. 100% equity ignores the role of debt/diversification even for a young investor. 50% equity ignores age-sensitivity altogether and would correspond to a much older investor under the same rule. Note: The NISM Series V-A workbook pages cited do not state the "100 minus age" formula as a rule; instead the workbook cautions that age alone may not be a prudent categorization basis and that allocation should be derived from risk profile, goals, situation and horizon. The "100 minus age" framing used above is presented as a general industry rule of thumb commonly referenced in personal finance, not as a workbook citation.
